picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Brief centers adaptogens and feeling good without a hangover, which maps to a buyer who tracks sleep and supplements and pays premiums (price_sensitivity: low). Her messaging preferences — ingredient transparency, outcome-focused — match the functional claims directly.
lean_into: ingredient transparency on the adaptogen blend
picks.ad_angle: The functional upgrade: adaptogens that let you wind down and still wake up sharp.

picks.name: The Gen Z Aesthete
picks.why_plausible: Functional_beverages is a listed affinity and she buys on self_treat and impulse, both top occasions in the brief. Brand values of playful and aesthetic match her preferences exactly.
lean_into: something to hold at the party that isn't a seltzer
avoid: anything that feels preachy about sobriety
picks.ad_angle: The best-looking drink in your hand all night — sober-curious as a vibe, not a sacrifice.

picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: Lists functional_beverages and recovery as affinities and works out 4+ times a week, so alcohol-free social drinking protects training. Price_sensitivity low-medium fits a premium can.
lean_into: identity: still social, still on plan
picks.ad_angle: Go out Saturday, still hit your Sunday session.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Urban millennial with mid-to-high income who buys on replenishment and impulse — a case of ready-to-drink cans is exactly a default-to-easy purchase. Brief's replenishment occasion fits his heavy repeat-buying habit.
lean_into: no mixing, no bar cart, just open
picks.ad_angle: Cocktail-grade in a can — zero prep, delivered by the case.

plan.summary: The one true beverage publisher is a competitor, so the plan runs on wellness adjacencies (Studiogrid, Pantrygood, Daily Form, Movewell) plus a high-reach late-night impulse test on Swiftcart, with Daily Form marked down for claim skepticism.

test.name: Studiogrid
test.adjustment_reason: Notes say users are 'actively spending on self-care and fitness', a strong post-workout/self-treat moment for an adaptogen drink that the low values score understates.
test.rationale: Studiogrid's notes describe an audience 'actively spending on self-care and fitness' with high income and a $42 booking AOV that matches the $40 offer almost exactly, making it the cleanest wellness adjacency in the set.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

test.risk: Appointment bookings are a service purchase, so confirmation-page intent to add a physical product is less proven than on a retail checkout.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.rationale: Pantrygood shoppers are 'responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims', which is exactly the language an adaptogen sparkling drink uses, and an $86 grocery basket makes a $40 add-on easy.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: Grocery subscribers may treat a premium single-SKU beverage as a duplicate of something already in their basket.

test.name: Movewell
test.rationale: Movewell pairs 22M impressions with 'fitness-engaged shoppers' in the brand's exact 25-44 age band, making it the volume play for a wellness beverage test.

evidence.quote: Fitness-engaged shoppers. Strong crossover with wellness and beauty

test.risk: Apparel checkout is a one-off fashion moment, so beverage relevance depends entirely on creative framing.

test.name: Swiftcart
test.adjacent_conflict: sells alcohol, soft_drinks, a close substitute
test.rationale: Swiftcart sells alcohol and has a 'late-night traffic spike', which is precisely the cocktail-replacement moment, and 84M impressions make it the cheapest place to learn; it stays a test because alcohol and soft drinks are a close substitute.
test.risk: Mid-income, 18-34 convenience buyers with a $28 basket may balk at a $40 premium beverage.

excluded.name: Pop & Sip
excluded.rationale: Direct competitor: Pop & Sip sells functional_beverages and soft drinks, the same shelf this drink competes on.

excluded.name: Daily Form
excluded.adjustment_reason: Notes warn the audience is 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims', which cuts against claims like 'Contains adaptogens' and 'No hangover' that the brief offers without substantiation.
excluded.rationale: Daily Form's supplement buyers overlap perfectly on wellness and price ($38 AOV vs $40 offer), but the notes say they are 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims' and the brief's adaptogen and no-hangover claims are unsupported.

evidence.quote: Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims

excluded.risk: Creative leaning on vague functional benefits will be picked apart by a science-forward audience; lead with ingredient specifics instead.

bid_strategy.rationale: $40 first order (assumed) × 0.30 = $12.00 target CPA: one-time purchase, so the first order has to pay back the acquisition. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed a premium price and about $40 first order, typical for functional drink multi-packs.
Assumed a broad adult audience aged roughly 25-44.
Assumed one-time purchase rather than subscription.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.
warnings: No publisher cleared the recommended bar, so the whole budget is a test. Treat results as exploratory.
Target CPA is based on an assumed order value. Confirm price before launch.
